short_definition: A minimum viable product (MVP) is the simplest version of a product that real customers can use, built to test whether a core idea solves a problem before investing heavily.
explanation: To build an MVP, identify the riskiest assumption behind your idea, usually whether people want it enough to pay, and build the smallest thing that tests it. That might be a landing page that takes pre-orders, a manually delivered 'concierge' version of a service or a basic prototype. You launch it to a small group, measure what they actually do and improve it in short cycles.

An MVP cuts the time and money spent building features nobody wants. Real customer behavior, such as sign-ups, payments and repeat use, is better evidence than opinions. Learning early also protects a young business's limited cash.

If an MVP is too bare or buggy, it can fail to show the idea's value. That gives you a false 'no' and can hurt your reputation. 'Viable' matters as much as 'minimum', and legal duties such as consumer protection, payment rules and data privacy still apply.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): Instead of spending $30,000 to build a meal-planning app, a founder spends $300 on a landing page and a weekly email meal plan priced at $8 a month. If 40 of 1,000 visitors (4%) pay within a month, there is evidence of demand. If almost nobody pays, she has learned that cheaply and can change the idea.
common_mistake: Spending months adding 'just one more feature' before launching. An MVP that never reaches real users isn't testing anything.
title: Minimum Viable Product (MVP)
